description: Four humours to DNA — how medical understanding of the body changed across 1,500 years.
content_html:
From Ancient Authority to Scientific Method

Medical knowledge in Britain between c.500 and the present day has been transformed by a succession of intellectual revolutions. For over a thousand years, the dominant framework was ancient Greek theory — particularly the works of Galen and the theory of the four humours. This began to be challenged in the sixteenth century, overthrown by germ theory in the nineteenth, and transformed again by molecular biology in the twentieth.

Galen and the Medieval Framework

Galen was a Greek physician who lived in the Roman Empire (c.129–c.216 AD). His prolific writings on anatomy, physiology and disease became the standard medical texts of medieval Europe, preserved and transmitted through the Islamic world to European universities. Galen taught that the body’s four humours governed health, that the liver produced blood, and that the heart attracted air through the lungs. Much of this was wrong — he worked largely from animal dissections rather than human ones — but the Church’s support for ancient authority meant his ideas went unchallenged for centuries. Medieval physicians were trained to reconcile patients’ symptoms with Galenic theory rather than to observe and question.

Key Fact

Galen’s works dominated European medicine from the medieval period until the sixteenth century. The Church’s backing of ancient authorities, combined with the rarity of books before printing, made it dangerous and difficult to challenge his theories.

Vesalius, Paré and Harvey: A New Anatomy

The sixteenth and seventeenth centuries saw the beginning of a systematic challenge to Galenic medicine, enabled by the Renaissance emphasis on observation and the printing press, which spread new ideas rapidly. Andreas Vesalius published his landmark work De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543. Based on his own careful dissections of human cadavers at the University of Padua, it corrected over 200 errors in Galen’s anatomy — demonstrating, for example, that the human jaw is a single bone (Galen had claimed it was two). Vesalius showed that medical knowledge must be grounded in direct observation.

Ambroise Paré (c.1510–1590), a French surgeon, developed new practical techniques for treating wounds. Rather than cauterising gunshot wounds with boiling oil (the standard treatment), he accidentally discovered that a simple salve was less harmful and led to better recovery. Paré also designed artificial limbs and improved ligation — tying blood vessels rather than burning them to stop bleeding after amputation. His work applied an empirical approach to surgical treatment.

The most significant advance of this period was William Harvey’s demonstration of the circulation of blood. Harvey, an English physician, published De Motu Cordis in 1628. Through systematic experiments — tying off veins and arteries and measuring the volume of blood pumped by the heart — he proved that blood circulates continuously around the body, pumped by the heart. This directly contradicted Galen, who believed blood was produced in the liver and consumed by the organs. Harvey’s work established experiment as the method of medical advance.

The transformation of medicine in the nineteenth century centred on germ theory. Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, published his germ theory in 1861, demonstrating that fermentation was caused by microorganisms and that spontaneous generation of life did not occur. German physician Robert Koch built on this in the 1870s and 1880s, developing techniques to isolate and culture specific bacteria and proving that particular bacteria caused particular diseases. Koch identified the bacterium causing anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883). Koch formulated a set of criteria — now known as Koch’s postulates — for establishing that a specific bacterium causes a specific disease. Germ theory provided the scientific basis for vaccines, antiseptics, antibiotics and the modern understanding of infection.

Scanning Technology: X-Rays, Ultrasound, MRI

The ability to see inside the living body without surgery transformed diagnosis in the twentieth century. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895; within months they were being used medically to reveal broken bones and foreign objects inside patients. Ultrasound imaging, developed from the 1950s and 1960s, used sound waves to create images of soft tissue — particularly valuable in obstetrics for monitoring foetal development. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), developed in the 1970s and 1980s, uses magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of organs and tissue without radiation. Together, these technologies enabled diagnosis of conditions that would previously have required exploratory surgery or been entirely invisible.

Key Fact

X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895. Ultrasound developed from the 1950s–1960s (especially valuable in monitoring pregnancy). MRI developed in the 1970s–1980s, providing detailed soft-tissue images without radiation. All three transformed the ability to diagnose disease without invasive surgery.

The most profound advance in medical knowledge in the twentieth century was the discovery of the structure of DNA. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick, working at Cambridge and drawing on X-ray crystallography data produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, published their model of the double helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). Understanding that DNA is the molecule of heredity opened the entire field of molecular biology and genetics. Scientists could now begin to understand why some diseases are inherited, how viruses replicate, and which genes are associated with cancer. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, mapped the full sequence of human DNA. This knowledge is enabling the development of targeted drug therapies and, in the future, possibly gene-editing treatments for inherited conditions.
exam_tip_html: For questions about advances in medical knowledge, you need to be clear about what was new and what it replaced. When writing about Vesalius or Harvey, explain what was wrong before (Galenic theory) and why the new knowledge was significant. For DNA and germ theory, link to broader consequences: germ theory enabled vaccines and antiseptics; DNA knowledge is enabling targeted therapies. Examiners reward responses that track the knock-on consequences of new knowledge, not just descriptions of the discovery itself.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Galen’s four humours and anatomical errors dominated European medicine for over 1,000 years; Vesalius (1543) and Harvey (1628) challenged and overturned key parts through direct observation and experiment.
  • Germ theory (Pasteur 1861; Koch 1870s–1890s) revolutionised understanding of disease by identifying specific microorganisms as causes of specific diseases, providing the scientific basis for vaccines, antiseptics and antibiotics.
  • The discovery of DNA by Watson and Crick in 1953 and the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003 opened a new era of molecular medicine, enabling genetic diagnosis and the development of targeted therapies.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the work of Andreas Vesalius.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Vesalius conducted systematic human dissections and published De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543, correcting over 200 errors in Galen's anatomy — such as showing the human jaw is a single bone, not two. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Robert Koch's contribution to medical knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Koch developed techniques to isolate and culture specific bacteria and proved that particular bacteria caused particular diseases, identifying the bacterium for tuberculosis in 1882 and cholera in 1883. Feature 2: Koch developed Koch's postulates — a set of criteria for proving a specific bacterium causes a specific disease — providing a scientific framework for bacteriology. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Galen's medical theories remained dominant in Europe for over 1,000 years.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one reason (e.g. Church backing of ancient authority; lack of printing to spread alternatives; training of physicians to reconcile observation with theory rather than to question it; absence of dissection due to religious restrictions) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear cause with evidence. Developing: Cause identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Harvey's discovery of the circulation of blood in 1628.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (directly contradicted Galen, demonstrated circulation vs liver-production, established experiment as the method) AND over time (foundation of understanding cardiovascular disease, surgical techniques, blood transfusion). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The discovery of germ theory was the most significant advance in medical knowledge in British history.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates germ theory's significance (enabled vaccines, antiseptics, antibiotics, public health reform) AND challenges with other candidates (Harvey's circulation, DNA double helix, scanning technology). Considers criteria for 'most significant'. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How did advances in medical knowledge change understanding of the body between c.1500 and the present day? Use evidence across the period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across early modern (Vesalius 1543, Harvey 1628), modern (Pasteur/Koch germ theory 1861–1890s, X-rays 1895), contemporary (Watson/Crick DNA 1953, Human Genome 2003). Weighs change against continuity (herbal and humoral elements persisted in popular medicine; alternative medicine today). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which work did Vesalius publish in 1543, correcting over 200 errors in Galen's anatomy?
When did Watson and Crick publish their model of the double helix structure of DNA?
William Harvey proved that blood _____ continuously around the body, directly contradicting Galen's theory that it was produced in the liver.
X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen in _____, transforming the ability to diagnose without invasive surgery.
Match each figure to their advance in medical knowledge:
right: Discovered the double helix structure of DNA in 1953
Ancient physician whose anatomical theories dominated medicine for 1,000 years
Developed germ theory, showing microorganisms cause disease, in 1861

flashcard_questions.q: What was the theory of the four humours?
flashcard_questions.a: The belief that health depended on balance among four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Vesalius publish De Humani Corporis Fabrica?
What was Vesalius's key method that Galen had not used for human anatomy?
What did William Harvey prove in De Motu Cordis (1628)?
flashcard_questions.a: That blood circulates continuously around the body, pumped by the heart.

flashcard_questions.q: What error in Galen did Harvey directly disprove?
flashcard_questions.a: That blood was produced in the liver and consumed by the organs.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Louis Pasteur publish germ theory?
Which three diseases did Koch identify the bacteria for in 1876–1883?
What is MRI scanning and when was it developed?
flashcard_questions.a: Magnetic Resonance Imaging using magnetic fields and radio waves; developed in the 1970s–1980s.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Watson and Crick publish their DNA double helix model?
When was the Human Genome Project completed?

flashcard_questions.a: The scientific theory that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.

glossary_terms.definition: An ancient Greek medical framework holding that the body contained four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance determined health.
A Greek physician (c.129–c.216 AD) whose anatomical and medical writings became the dominant authority in European medicine for over 1,000 years.
A Flemish anatomist (1514–1564) who conducted systematic human dissections and published De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543, correcting numerous errors in Galen.
The scientific theory, developed by Pasteur and Koch, that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
The molecule that carries the genetic instructions for the growth, development, functioning and reproduction of all living organisms.
